claims.text: Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported yield strength of 786 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported terminal strain of 13.5%.
Adding approximately 2 at.% Al and applying the specified two-step heat treatment will produce a duplex microstructure.
The modified microstructure will retain a high-strength BCC matrix.
The treatment will form a thin, discontinuous, Al-enriched ductile phase at grain boundaries.
Al selectively segregates to grain boundaries during the proposed heat treatment.
The proposed grain-boundary film enhances intergranular cohesion and local plasticity.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and plasticity will distribute tensile strain more uniformly.
The proposed grain-boundary film will delay intergranular crack initiation under tensile loading.
The modified alloy will retain the matrix's high intrinsic lattice resistance.
Controlling the heat treatment will minimize formation of detrimental thick intermetallic phases.
The modified alloy will achieve more than 20% tensile uniform elongation at room temperature and approximately 10^-4 s^-1.
Tensile uniform elongation will improve by at least 50% relative to the stated 13.5% baseline strain.
The modified alloy will maintain tensile yield strength above approximately 750 MPa.
The modified alloy will maintain compressive strength above approximately 1250 MPa.
The modified alloy will retain or exceed the baseline impact-triggered energy release at approximately 10^3 s^-1.
The hypothesis is limited to room-temperature quasi-static tension and compression near 10^-4 s^-1 and impact loading near 10^3 s^-1.
The hypothesis is untested at elevated temperatures and outside the stated strain-rate limits.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says strength will not be compromised, but the acceptance thresholds of >750 MPa yield strength and >1250 MPa compressive strength permit decreases from the stated baselines of 786 and 1314 MPa.

The prediction treats the reported 13.5% terminal strain as the baseline for tensile uniform elongation, although terminal strain and uniform tensile elongation are distinct measures and the baseline loading mode is not identified.
The predicted outcome requires retained or increased impact energy release, whereas the falsification rule only rejects a significant reduction, potentially allowing a smaller reduction.
